subsection: 9. Culture and religion: the Irish language, Vatican II and the communications revolution

notes.b: The language was official policy in the Republic but was losing ground among the population, and campaigns in the 1950s and 1960s pushed for change in how it was taught and promoted.
points: The Constitution of 1937 declared Irish the national language and the first official language of the state, but few people used it in daily life outside the Gaeltacht areas.
Gael Linn was founded in 1953 to promote Irish through cultural and commercial projects, including the Irish-language films and records it produced.
Compulsory Irish was a requirement for a Leaving Certificate pass, and critics argued that it turned many pupils away from the language.
The Language Freedom Movement, founded in 1966, campaigned for the end of compulsory Irish in schools and for the freedom of choice in language teaching.
Compulsory Irish for a Leaving Certificate pass was abolished in 1973, which was a major change in education and in public attitudes to the language.
Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting in October 1972, giving Irish speakers in the Gaeltacht a regular service in their own language.
Bord na Gaeilge was set up in 1975 to promote the use of Irish in daily life and to develop Irish-language media and services.
The Gaeltacht areas were in decline through the 1950s and 1960s, with emigration and English-language media reducing use of the language in the west.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, founded in 1951, promoted traditional music, dance and language through local branches and competitions.
Seán Ó Riada's composition Mise Éire (1959) and his work with the Ceoltóirí Chualann ensemble brought Irish traditional music to wider audiences and into the concert hall.
The traditional music revival of the 1960s and 1970s helped create a national market for Irish folk and traditional music.

notes.h: Vatican II and the Irish Church
notes.b: The Second Vatican Council, held in Rome from 1962 to 1965, changed Catholic worship and the church's relations with other Christians and with the modern world.
points: The council allowed the mass to be said in the vernacular, which in Ireland meant English for most congregations and Irish in the Gaeltacht.
It encouraged lay participation in the liturgy, including roles for lay readers and eucharistic ministers, which changed the role of the parish.
It promoted ecumenism, which means closer relations and dialogue between Catholics and other Christian churches, and this encouraged new contacts between Catholic and Protestant churches in Ireland.
It stated that religious liberty was a human right, which challenged the claim of the Catholic Church to a privileged position in the state.
The decline in vocations to the priesthood and religious life through the 1960s and 1970s reflected changing attitudes to the church and to religious careers.

notes.h: Key personality: Archbishop John Charles McQuaid, part 2
notes.b: McQuaid was Archbishop of Dublin from 1940 to 1972, and his response to Vatican II was a central test of the church's authority in the 1960s.
points: McQuaid was a leading member of the Irish hierarchy at the council, and he supported its reforms but was cautious about their pace and their effect on Irish practice.
He oversaw the introduction of the vernacular mass in Dublin and the rest of the country, though he resisted some changes that he saw as weakening traditional devotion.
Contemporaries saw him as the most powerful churchman in Ireland, and his influence on public policy, including the Mother and Child Scheme of 1951, was widely recognised.
Contemporary attitudes were divided: many lay Catholics welcomed the council's reforms, while traditionalists saw McQuaid as too slow to change.
Historians judge him as a conservative leader who presided over the end of the church's public dominance but could not stop the decline in its authority.
The Censorship of Publications Act 1929 banned books and magazines considered indecent or obscene, and enforcement remained strict through the 1950s.
Censorship was relaxed in 1967 when the government amended the rules, allowing a wider range of books and films to be published and shown in Ireland.
Secularisation, the decline in the influence of religion on public life, grew in the 1960s and 1970s as church attendance and the role of religious ideas in politics declined.
The debates over divorce and contraception in the 1980s showed that secular and religious views remained sharply opposed (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).

notes.b: Ó hEithir was a writer and broadcaster who used Irish and English to explore rural life and the changing identity of the Gaeltacht.
points: Breandán Ó hEithir wrote in Irish and English and was a leading voice in the Irish-language literary world from the 1950s onwards.
His best-known work, the memoir Over the Bog (1959), described life in a rural Gaeltacht community and was widely read in both languages (verify title and date).
As a broadcaster with RTÉ, he presented programmes in Irish and English that brought the language and rural life to a national audience.
Contemporaries valued his work as a bridge between the Gaeltacht and urban Ireland, though some critics felt his portrayal of rural life was nostalgic.
Historians see him as an important figure in the Irish-language revival of the period, and in the wider debate over identity, language and modernisation.
The spread of telephones, newspapers, radio and later television from the 1950s changed how Irish people received news and entertainment.
Car ownership and better road transport reduced the isolation of rural communities and increased their links with towns and cities.
Computers and new technologies were introduced into business and government in the 1970s and 1980s, changing work and the flow of information.
Access to British and American media, through radio and later television, exposed Irish people to a wider range of views and cultural norms.
Achievements: the Irish language gained official and institutional support through Bord na Gaeilge and Raidió na Gaeltachta, and Irish music achieved wide popularity.
Limits: the Irish language remained in decline as a community language, especially in the Gaeltacht, and the revival of the 1960s did not reverse this trend.
Contemporary view: traditionalists saw the reforms of the 1960s as a threat to Irish identity and Catholic values, while reformers saw them as overdue.
Later view: historians see the period as the start of secularisation and pluralism in Irish culture, though the church kept a strong influence on public life into the 1980s.
